title: The forgotten formula for lovable cities - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Revisits Camillo Sitte's 1889 The Art of Building Cities, arguing that lovable cities come from enclosed, small, asymmetric spaces with monuments at edges and landmarks embedded in vernacular fabric — not from beautiful facades. After being eclipsed by modernism, Sitte's principles are being revived by New Urbanists and infill architects, though mainstream development applies them clumsily.

themes.theme: Sitte's core thesis: space, not facades, drives lovability

insights.claim: Camillo Sitte's 1889 book The Art of Building Cities argues the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating shelter, intimacy, framed views, and making public buildings look larger by comparison.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Urban-design value is driven by spatial layout, not just architecture — relevant to how placemaking premiums are created in real-estate development.
insights.quote: the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small
insights.locator: The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte

insights.claim: Streets in modern Asian cities such as Osaka, Taipei and Hong Kong are loved despite mostly nondescript modern buildings, implying that street character comes from spatial form rather than historic architecture.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Lovable, high-footfall districts can be built with ordinary modern buildings if layout is right — lowers the cost of creating desirable neighborhoods.
insights.locator: Everyone loves the streets of old

insights.claim: The article argues that focusing only on the appearance of buildings is insufficient; neighborhoods following Sittean principles can be charming even if their individual buildings are unremarkable, while world-class buildings can be let down by poor surroundings.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Developers and planners chasing 'beauty' via facades alone may misallocate capital; layout is the cheaper lever.
insights.quote: neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special
insights.locator: Sitte’s attacks were directed against

themes.theme: Enclosure mechanics: turbine squares, bridged entrances, terminated streets

insights.claim: Sitte framed enclosed squares as 'outdoor rooms'; a city without them is like an extreme open-plan house where rooms bleed into each other's character.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A usable mental model for evaluating masterplans: count how many spaces read as distinct 'rooms'.
insights.locator: Create enclosed spaces

insights.claim: Brussels' Grand-Place preserves enclosure with a 'turbine square' layout: one street per corner, continuing the plane of the square's side so entrances are virtually invisible from inside; Sitte called this a conscious or subconscious principle of ancient city building.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Specific, replicable design device that can be specified in new developments at near-zero cost.
insights.quote: it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building
insights.locator: The picture above shows the Grand-Place

insights.claim: Barcelona's Plaça Reial has seven entrances, six of which are bridged over, making it feel like a courtyard; Sitte considered bridged entrances and colonnades greatly underrated tools for enclosure.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Colonnades/bridging are low-tech ways to retrofit enclosure onto existing squares.
insights.locator: Even better than a turbine square

insights.claim: Trafalgar Square in London and the Place de la Concorde in Paris (nine roads, buildings on only one side) are weakly enclosed because they were designed around traffic flow, making them bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Traffic-optimized nodes degrade pedestrian value — a recurring pattern behind pedestrianization and road-diet projects.
insights.quote: The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians
insights.locator: An even more extreme example

insights.claim: Curves and T-junctions visually terminate streets: Manhattan's curving Broad Street, closed by Federal Hall National Memorial, feels like an enclosed square, while 42nd Street reads as an endless corridor of 'parallels vanishing at infinity'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Grid plans systematically under-produce memorable spaces; curved/terminated streets are a differentiator for new districts.
insights.locator: Sitte applied this logic to streets

themes.theme: Scale rules: squares should be small relative to buildings

insights.claim: Sitte's rule of thumb: a square's dimensions should be no greater than twice the height of its principal building.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A quantifiable design rule that can be applied to evaluate public-realm proposals.
insights.quote: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it
insights.locator: If a square is too large

insights.claim: Over-large squares such as the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest make their monumental buildings look like doll's houses and leave visitors feeling exposed; making buildings taller instead produces inhumanly huge structures, as at Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Bigger is not grander: oversized civic spaces destroy the value they intend to showcase.
insights.locator: If a square is too large

insights.claim: Bernini's St Peter’s Square in the Vatican is argued to be far too large: impressive in drone footage but exhausting at ground level, making the Basilica look small and stubby and leaving visitors huddling under colonnades in summer heat.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Design optimized for aerial/plan views (and now drone/social imagery) can diverge from lived experience — a trap for showcase projects.
insights.locator: Some of the world’s most famous squares

insights.claim: The small square in front of Rome's Pantheon magnifies it: though smaller than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, it is larger relative to its square and retains dignity even though street level has risen 1.3 meters since Antiquity.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Relative scale, not absolute size, determines perceived grandeur.
insights.locator: By contrast, the small square

insights.claim: Sitte argued symmetry is overrated because pedestrians rarely stand at the point where symmetry is perceived; the octagonal Place Vendôme in Paris is striking from above but can feel awkward at ground level, whereas Verona's irregular pentagonal Piazza delle Erbe reads as harmonious.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Plan-view neatness is a poor proxy for experiential quality — challenges masterplanning-by-diagram.
insights.locator: Above is the Piazza delle Erbe

insights.claim: Irregularities in squares subtly arouse visual interest and create recesses that can host resting places, statues or public art, per Sitte.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Irregular sites need not be a development penalty; they can be an amenity.
insights.locator: Above is the Piazza delle Erbe

insights.claim: Monuments should go at the edges of squares, against neutral backdrops, not in the center or on axes with key buildings; Florence's Piazza della Signoria lines statues along its sides, letting Michelangelo’s David replica stand out against the Palazzo Vecchio.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Placement rules for public art affect both foot traffic and the perceived value of the art itself.
insights.locator: Move monuments to the edges

insights.claim: London's Victoria Memorial, centered on the Mall's axis, blocks the view of Buckingham Palace and its outline clashes with the palace detailing — a defect unnoticed only because centered siting is so common.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Conventional practice can embed persistent, unexamined design errors.
insights.locator: Later planners became fascinated

insights.claim: A bronze David over five meters tall on Florence's Piazzale Michelangelo looks miniaturized because, isolated against the sky, it lacks comparators; walls behind sculpture provide a visual key that makes it look bigger.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Perceived scale depends on context — relevant for any landmark or signage investment.
insights.quote: when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess
insights.locator: Isolating statues against the sky

insights.claim: Sitte disliked museums, calling them 'art prisons', and envisioned a city teeming with art woven into ordinary civic life.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Signals an alternative model of public art embedded in the street, relevant to cultural-district planning.
insights.locator: In Sitte’s view, the plain edge

insights.claim: Of the 255 churches of Rome, Sitte counted 41 adjoining other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three and two on all four; only six were freestanding, two of them modern Protestant churches.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Hard historical evidence that embedding monuments in ordinary fabric was the norm, not the exception.
insights.quote: Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four.
insights.locator: Sitte’s view on buildings was similar

insights.claim: Nineteenth-century dégagement — demolishing vernacular buildings around monuments — backfired: Haussmann's clearing of Rue Neuve Notre Dame to create the Parvis Notre-Dame made Notre Dame look smaller and lonelier by removing framing, scale contrast and the dramatic close-up reveal.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Clearance-based 'showcasing' destroys value; infill around landmarks may raise it.
insights.quote: Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.
insights.locator: For example, Notre Dame Cathedral

insights.claim: Sitte proposed infilling the 'desolate monster plaza' around Vienna's Votive Church with regular urban fabric defining three small squares; the article notes the scheme's density and spatial efficiency, though it was never implemented.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Aesthetic and density goals can align: infilling oversized civic voids adds developable land and improves the landmark.
insights.quote: Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.
insights.locator: Sitte thought that cities should move

insights.claim: Padua and Washington DC represent a figure-ground inversion: in Padua buildings are molded around spaces, while in Washington space is molded around freestanding monumental buildings.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A quick diagnostic lens for comparing urban plans and their likely pedestrian appeal.
insights.quote: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings
insights.locator: Another way to understand this contrast

themes.theme: Rise, fall and revival of Sitte's ideas

insights.claim: The Art of Building Cities prompted redrawn urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria within a year of publication, and by Sitte's death in 1903 his advocates held prominent posts in Munich, Berlin and Vienna.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows how fast a compelling design framework can reshape planning practice.
insights.quote: ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’
insights.locator: The rise, fall, and rise of Camillo Sitte

insights.claim: Helsinki switched from a neoclassical grid to Sittesque planning in the early twentieth century, producing characterful 'old town' effects even with the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as before.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Evidence that layout alone, holding density and building type constant, can create charm — density and lovability are compatible.
insights.quote: even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor
insights.locator: Two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate

insights.claim: Modernism eclipsed Sitte by treating public space as leftover, favoring parallel blocks over perimeter blocks and reducing built footprint for greenery, parking and roads; critic Sigfried Giedion dismissed Sitte as an ineffectual 'troubadour'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains the low baseline quality of mid-century urban fabric that today's regeneration targets.
insights.quote: ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’
insights.locator: Modernists also wanted to reduce

insights.claim: The article argues modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide, vindicating Sitte: New Urbanist towns Seaside, I’On and Poundbury were explicitly designed under his influence, and practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque infill schemes, including an Ash Sakula plan for a derelict Norwich shopping center.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Sittesque, traditional-street design is the ascendant paradigm — watch for it in regeneration of dead retail sites and new towns.
insights.locator: Ironically, modernism proved

insights.claim: Mainstream development is moving toward traditional streets and squares, but slowly and often incompetently, with many recent attempts looking awkward or stilted; the article argues studying Sitte can help relearn a lost art.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Execution gap in 'traditional' development creates an edge for designers/developers who master the actual principles.
insights.quote: Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently.
insights.locator: Mainstream development is moving
